newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Clinton plants tree to honour apartheid's victims.
newsitem.headline: Clinton plants tree to honour apartheid's victims.

text.p: U.S. first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton on Wednesday praised black South Africans for their willingness to forgive the country's former white rulers as she helped dedicate a garden to victims of apartheid.

"What you are doing here in South Africa is a testament to what can occur when rage and anger are turned to hope and possibility," Mrs. Clinton said in a speech to ex-political prisoners, survivors of human rights violations and relatives of some who died in racial unrest.

She was speaking at the dedication for the "Garden of Remembrance" at the foot of towering Table Mountain. She and South African Nobel peace laureate Desmond Tutu planted an indigenous stinkwood tree to remember the victims and unveiled a commemorative stone made of Table Mountain sandstone.
"Now it is time to heal the wounds of the past," Tutu told the gathering. "Now it is time to plant seeds of hope for the future."

The dedication ceremony came after Mrs. Clinton and her daughter Chelsea, on the second day of a three-day trip to South Africa, met Tutu and other members of the country's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, a body investigating human rights abuses by both pro-apartheid and anti-apartheid activists.

Mrs. Clinton said it was understandable if parents or loved ones of the victims had turned to "hatred, bitterness, anger or violence," but instead, "they forgave and are here today in that spirit of forgiveness and rememberence".

"The work of reconciliation is to acknowledge history, not to forget it, no matter how tragic, and to pass that history on to our children because only that has the power to arm them and all humanity," she added.

Tutu, 65 and a leading campaigner in the struggle against the former racist government, heads the Commission. He said said Mrs. Clinton had said during the meeting that a symbol of reconciliation might help, citing the United States' Vietnam War Memorial as a way her own country had sought to come to terms with painful episodes of its history.
The day was clouded by news that Tutu's prostate cancer appears to have spread to to other parts of his body and he is now going to the United States for radiation therapy.

However, Tutu shrugged off the news with a joke and said it would not interfere with the Commission's work. Tutu quipped that he had colleagues who were "very, very competent people. I am able to get away and look good because of them."

Mrs. Clinton was expected to strike similar themes of forgiveness and reconciliation in a speech Thursday at the University of Cape Town. She will also meet South African President Nelson Mandela and together they will visit the Robben Island prison cell where he was imprisoned under the apartheid government.
Earlier on Wednesday she visited the Victoria Mxenge homes project and was greeted by crowds of ululating women.

The development is one of many being undertaken in post- apartheid South Africa to try to get proper homes to an estimated one million people who live in poverty, many of them in dense "squatter towns."

The visit to the project emphasised a key goal of her two- week tour of six countries in Africa -- promoting better rights and education for women and children. Of 268 people working at the site, 260 were women.
"You are not only building houses, you are building your country," Mrs. Clinton told them.
